items.title: Ford's $5 day was a retention crisis fix, not generosity
items.claim: In January 1914, Henry Ford doubled the basic wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day. What problem was he solving?

options.text: Falling demand for the Model T
Catastrophic worker turnover — the assembly line was so monotonous that annual turnover had reached around 370%, meaning the plant had to hire roughly 50,000 people to maintain a workforce of 14,000
A unionisation drive he wanted to prevent

items.reveal:
Daniel Raff and Lawrence Summers's 1987 paper analysed Ford's wage decision. Turnover collapsed after the announcement; absenteeism dropped from 10% to 2.5%; productivity rose. The wage was conditional — there was a 'Sociological Department' that inspected workers' homes for 'good moral character' to qualify.

The popular story (Ford paid workers enough to buy his cars) is a post-hoc rationalisation. A Model T cost roughly $440; a workforce of 14,000 buying cars wouldn't move the market.

The wage was efficient: Ford gained productivity worth more than the extra wage bill.
items.why: Famous 'visionary' business decisions usually have boring, specific operational drivers. The $5 day looks like generosity; it was wage-efficiency arbitrage.

items.title: Patagonia's owner gave the company to the planet
items.claim: In September 2022, Yvon Chouinard announced he was transferring ownership of Patagonia. What was the structure?

options.text: An IPO on the New York Stock Exchange
All voting stock to the Patagonia Purpose Trust (climate-aligned governance); all non-voting stock (98%) to the Holdfast Collective, with future profits funding environmental causes
A sale to a private equity buyer

items.reveal:
Chouinard, his wife Malinda and their two children transferred Patagonia (valued around $3bn) using two vehicles: the Purpose Trust holds voting control to ensure mission alignment; the Holdfast Collective (a 501(c)(4) nonprofit) holds economic ownership and receives roughly $100m of annual profits to fund environmental work.

The structure required the family to pay $17.5m in gift tax. The company is a B Corp (certified since 2011) — the legal structure goes much further than B Corp certification alone.

B Lab's B Corp movement, launched in 2006, certifies firms meeting social and environmental performance standards.
items.why: Corporate ownership structures shape objectives. A trust-owned firm doesn't have to maximise shareholder returns — because its 'shareholders' are not the same as a public company's.

items.title: CSR and financial performance — the evidence is mixed but tilts positive
items.claim: Friede, Busch and Bassen's 2015 meta-analysis aggregated over 2,000 studies on the link between ESG (environmental, social, governance) factors and corporate financial performance. What did it find?

options.text: ESG and financial performance are negatively related across the board
Around 90% of studies found a non-negative relationship; the majority showed positive correlation between ESG performance and financial performance, though magnitudes are modest
No study has examined this question
ESG is required to be at least cost-neutral by law

items.reveal:
Friede, Busch and Bassen (Journal of Sustainable Finance and Investment, 2015) reviewed 2,200 empirical studies dating back to the 1970s. About 90% reported non-negative ESG-CFP relationships; ~63% reported positive.

Milton Friedman's 1970 New York Times Magazine essay ('The Social Responsibility of Business is to Increase its Profits') argued the opposite. The empirical question turns out to be less stark than either side claims — the effect is usually positive but small, and depends on which ESG element and which industry.
items.why: Strategy debates about CSR are often conducted without reference to the evidence. The aggregate finding is messier than either 'CSR is profitable' or 'CSR is a cost' implies.
